documents.abstract: Abstract Background The registry record of psychedelic and related rapid-acting compounds is large, heterogeneous and laborious to synthesize by hand. We tested whether a large language model (LLM) with live access to the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface (API) could produce a timely, structured and reproducible characterization of this landscape. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of interventional trials on ClinicalTrials.gov as of 13 January 2026. The core-set comprised classic serotonin 5-HT2A agonists, MDMA, ibogaine and ayahuasca; ketamine and esketamine in psychiatric indications formed a separately reported comparator class. Claude (Anthropic), connected to the registry API, retrieved records first through open-ended natural-language querying and then through a documented protocol of field-specific query expressions restricted to records first posted by the search date, which yielded every reported count; populations and indications were defined from structured registry fields. Results Excluding withdrawn records, 412 core-set trials were identified (256 in patients), plus 300 ketamine/esketamine trials. Psilocybin accounted for 244 (59%; 181 in patients), MDMA 99 (47), LSD 39 (13), DMT/5-MeO-DMT 36 (12), ayahuasca 6 and ibogaine 4. Depression led for psilocybin (74 of 181 patient trials) and the ketamine class (237 of 300), PTSD for MDMA (35 of 47) and anxiety for LSD (6 of 13). Of 63 phase 2/3 psilocybin trials in depression, 35 (56%) had a depression rating scale as primary endpoint, most often the MADRS (25), 34 (54%) assessed it at weeks 3–6, 26 (41%) excluded adults over 65 and none enrolled adolescents. Twenty-four core-set trials were registered as phase 3, 13 of psilocybin; psilocybin phase 3 programmes plan more than 1900 participants, the pivotal MDMA trials enrolled 100 and 121, LSD phase 3 trials plan 149–245, and no other psychedelic had a phase 3 trial. Five patient trials (2%) had a site in a low- or middle-income country. Conclusions LLM-mediated registry querying yielded a structured, reproducible characterization of a fast-moving field, but only once each count was tied to an explicit, archived query expression; open-ended conversational querying had underestimated the record several-fold for some compounds. The approach complements rather than replaces systematic review, and its accuracy against manual extraction remains to be quantified.

Background/Objectives: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by alterations in brain development and function, frequently associated with complex genetic architectures. The widespread implementation of next-generation sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing (WES), has substantially increased the identification of potentially disease-associated variants, shifting the major challenge from variant detection to their interpretation and prioritization. This review examines the emerging contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to WES variant interpretation in NDDs, with particular emphasis on AI-assisted variant prioritization and protein structural modelling. Methods: We reviewed conventional computational and emerging AI-driven approaches applicable to different stages of WES interpretation, including variant pathogenicity and functional-effect prediction, evolutionary conservation, splicing assessment, phenotype-informed prioritization, and protein structure prediction. Their methodological principles, applications, and major limitations were critically examined within the context of neurodevelopmental genomics. Results: AI and machine-learning approaches increasingly integrate genomic, phenotypic, functional, and structural information, supporting phenotype-aware candidate prioritization and molecular contextualization of selected variants. However, computational outputs are affected by model-specific limitations and should not be considered independent evidence of pathogenicity. Their added value depends primarily on the complementarity and biological relevance of the information provided, rather than on predictor concordance alone. Conclusions: This narrative review highlights that AI-assisted WES interpretation should prioritize complementary, mechanism-relevant evidence over computational concordance. AI-assisted tools should therefore be selected according to variant class and disease mechanism and integrated with independent clinical, genetic, and functional evidence.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) continuously opens up new possibilities in film post-production, including the subsequent relighting of moving images. As a systematic assessment from a film-design and professional-practice perspective has been lacking, this study examines the potentials, limitations, and implications of current AI-based relighting workflows for cinematographic practice. Methodologically, the study follows a qualitative-exploratory research design within practice-based and practice-led frameworks. Three current AI-based relighting systems (Nvidia DiffusionRenderer, Beeble Studio, and SwitchX) were tested across five test shots and evaluated using a cinematography-oriented qualitative evaluation scheme focusing on light plausibility, image quality and texture retention, as well as image integrity and temporal stability. These observations were complemented by eight semi-structured expert interviews with professionals from cinematography, lighting, and color grading. Results suggest that AI-based relighting does not currently replace on-set lighting but offers considerable potential as a selective correction and extension tool. Its strengths are particularly evident in wide and establishing shots, where faces and fine image details are less perceptually salient, as well as in situations where the desired lighting conditions are difficult to achieve or maintain on set due to weather, time, or budget constraints. Technical and creative limitations are most apparent in workflow integration and usability, as well as in texture loss and image alterations that impair visual credibility, particularly in portrait shots. The findings suggest the potential for a selective shift of certain lighting decisions toward post-production rather than a general replacement of on-set lighting. To maintain a coherent lighting design when substantial lighting decisions are deferred to post-production, greater continuity of cinematographic expertise and creative agency across production and post-production may be required.

The AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System is an artificial intelligence-based web application developed to help students and job seekers improve their interview skills through interactive mock interviews, automated performance evaluation, and personalized feedback. In today’s competitive employment environment, candidates often face challenges such as nervousness, poor communication skills, lack of confidence, and insufficient interview practice. Traditional preparation methods may not provide immediate and consistent feedback, creating a need for an intelligent system that supports effective and personalized interview preparation. The proposed system integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to support interview practice and analyze candidate responses. It provides job-role-based interview preparation, maintains interview history, and helps users identify their strengths and weaknesses through feedback. The application consists of two main modules: the Admin Module and the Student Module. The Admin Module manages student information, job roles, interviews, and feedback, while the Student Module allows users to access their dashboard, practice interviews, review previous sessions, view feedback, and manage their profiles. The system aims to provide an accessible and structured environment for continuous learning and performance improvement. By combining AI-based assessment with a user-friendly web interface, the AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System can help candidates develop better communication skills, increase confidence, and improve their readiness for real-world job interviews. Future enhancements may include advanced speech analysis, facial expression recognition, body-language assessment, multilingual support, and more comprehensive real-time performance evaluation

We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The instruments used for intraoperative guidance have not improved over the years. Traditional margin evaluations fail in 10–20% of cancer surgeries, and histopathology confirmation can take 48–72 h. A promising alternative is hyperspectral imaging (HSI), which allows for real-time, label-free, non-contact, and detailed biochemical characterization of tissues. This review synthesizes 130 studies from 2015 to 2026, identified through a systematic search across multiple databases following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The studies cover various clinical areas, including surgical oncology (53%), neurosurgery (10.8%), perfusion assessment (6.2%), gastroenterology (5.4%), dermatology (4.6%), and emerging domains (20%). Each clinical area is evaluated using a four-part Translational Readiness Appraisal framework. This framework shifts the focus from technical proficiency to deployment evidence by examining hardware compatibility with operating rooms, real-time workflow integration, cross-site validation, and regulatory readiness. Since 2015, the combination of clinically approved HSI hardware and artificial intelligence has led to a tenfold increase in publications. However, a significant gap remains: none of the reviewed studies meet the evidence criteria necessary for regulatory approval. Of the studies, 48.5% show strong single-site validation, but 50.8% remain in the proof-of-concept stage. The heavy reliance on intra-patient validation tends to inflate performance estimates, leaving issues like calibration across devices and regulatory pathways largely unaddressed. HSI has demonstrated technical maturity in several areas, particularly in head and neck margin assessment and brain tumor delineation. The primary reason for the lack of clinical adoption is not imaging performance but rather the absence of multicenter validation and a formal regulatory evidence framework.
topics: Spectroscopy Techniques in Biomedical and Chemical Research

documents.abstract: The need for precise lithium-ion battery (LiB) monitoring and prognostics has grown significantly with the increasing use of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy system (RES) technologies. State of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), and remaining useful life (RUL) are three critical performance metrics for ensuring battery safety, functional dependability, and effective energy utilization. Non-linear degradation patterns, operating uncertainties, and dynamic environmental fluctuations are frequently difficult for traditional electrochemical and empirical assessment methods to capture. As a result, recent research has focused on advanced data-driven techniques for comprehensive battery state estimation, notably those based on artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning (DL). This review provides an overview of current methodologies for SOC, SOH, and RUL prediction, with a focus on modern DL architectures such as transformer networks, autoencoder-based latent modeling, neural basis expansion techniques, attention mechanisms, and hybrid optimization-driven frameworks. The article examines new advances in intelligent battery prognostics critically, emphasizing their potential for improved estimation precision, resilience, and flexibility in practical operating scenarios. In addition, it identifies future research directions such as enhanced optimization-assisted frameworks, hybrid physics-informed learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). This article intends to offer a comprehensive overview of modern battery prognostics approaches to aid in the development of dependable, efficient, and long-term battery management system (BMS) solutions for electric mobility and energy storage systems.

Senior High School (SHS) students often face challenges in selecting the most appropriate academic strand due to limited assessment tools and the continued reliance on traditional guidance practices. These methods frequently lack objectivity and comprehensive evaluation, resulting in mismatches between students’ competencies, interests, and their chosen academic pathways. Such misalignment may affect students’ academic performance, educational direction, and future career readiness. This study aimed to develop an AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System designed to objectively evaluate student competencies and generate strand recommendations that align with learners’ abilities, interests, and career potential. The system intends to support students, teachers, and guidance personnel by providing data-driven insights that can assist in making informed academic decisions. The research employed a quantitative–descriptive design integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The system was developed using an Input–Process–Output (IPO) conceptual framework combined with Agile Software Development Methodology, enabling iterative system improvement and structured data processing. The platform utilizes a 30-dimension assessment model measuring cognitive skills, literacy and communication abilities, technical aptitude, and personality-interest indicators. Student responses are processed through a structured scoring model and analyzed using an AI-powered evaluation module to generate strand recommendations, competency profiles, and career-related insights, which are presented in a downloadable evaluation report. The results are presented in a comprehensive evaluation report that users can download and use for academic guidance and decision-making. Evaluation results showed strong system performance and user acceptance. Based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, IT experts gave the system an overall mean score of 3.95, indicating a high level of software quality and functionality. System users rated the platform with an overall mean score of 4.00, interpreted as Highly Acceptable, reflecting positive user experience and effectiveness. This finding clearly demonstrates that the system can provide data-driven guidance in SHS strand selection, reduce academic-career mismatches, and support better educational alignment and long-term career readiness among students.

This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence in advancing personalised disability support within higher education. It analyses key applications, including adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and assistive technologies, highlighting their capacity to improve access, engagement, and student success. Attention is given to opportunities for enhancing institutional performance through data-informed decision-making and scalable support systems. Ethical considerations, including transparency, fairness, privacy, and user autonomy, are critically explored, alongside the importance of human-centred and participatory design approaches. The chapter further discusses governance, policy alignment, and capacity building as essential conditions for responsible AI integration. It argues that the transformative potential of AI depends on sustained institutional commitment to inclusive, equitable, and ethically grounded practices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning models provide powerful data-driven tools for modeling complex nonlinear systems and predicting process behavior from limited experimental data. In this study, an AI-driven predictive framework is developed for modeling paracetamol solubility and solvent density in supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO 2 ). A dataset comprising 40 experimental observations was employed, with pressure and temperature used as input variables and paracetamol mole fraction and SC-CO 2 density considered as target outputs. Three machine-learning regression algorithms—Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Tweedie Regression (TDR), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)—were developed and comparatively evaluated. To enhance predictive performance and automate model configuration, the Cheetah Optimizer (CO), a nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithm, was integrated into the modeling framework for hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), mean squared error (MSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). The results demonstrated that TDR provided the highest predictive accuracy for paracetamol mole fraction, achieving an R 2 of 0.985, whereas GPR exhibited the best performance for SC-CO 2 density prediction, with an R 2 of 0.991. The developed framework successfully captured the nonlinear relationships between operating conditions and the predicted properties while demonstrating that the optimal learning algorithm depends on the target variable. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted optimization and machine-learning approaches for data-driven prediction and intelligent modeling of complex supercritical-fluid processes.

The current study has been conducted to propose and validate the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven banking ecosystem model for understanding how AI improves customer experience, risk management, and operational efficiency within the context of the banking industry. Specifically, the study aims to overcome the lack of empirical studies providing holistic evidence on how AI works in emerging regional banking markets by analysing the influence of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness on banking performance. The study utilises quantitative and explanatory research designs and data collection procedures. In total, 480 participants, including customers, employees, and branch managers of scheduled commercial banks have been surveyed. The AI-driven banking ecosystem has been defined using the constructs of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness. Descriptive statistics, reliability and validity testing, CFA, and SEM have been used for data analysis. The findings show that the AI-driven banking ecosystem positively influences all dimensions of banking performance. In addition, risk management (β = 0.751, p < 0.001), operational efficiency (β = 0.704, p < 0.001), and customer experience (β = 0.582, p < 0.01) had the highest impact on performance in the banking industry. The structural model presented satisfactory goodness-of-fit indicators, which confirmed the conceptual framework of the research and all the hypotheses of the study. In addition, the research suggests the development of an integrated AI driven banking ecosystem framework that takes into account technological, organisational, and strategic aspects of AI.

This chapter delves into the transformative synergy between artificial intelligence (AI) and smart contracts, positioning them as the next frontier in managing digital assets and virtual currencies. It introduces the core concepts, illustrating how AI injects adaptability into rigid blockchain-based contracts, enabling real-time adjustments, predictive analytics, and autonomous dispute resolution. From an economic perspective, the integration drives efficiency in decentralized finance (DeFi), with the total value locked surging to $129 billion by mid-2025, thereby democratizing access while posing risks such as market bubbles. Socially, it promises inclusion for underserved populations through microlending and empowers communities via decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), yet raises concerns over biases, job disruptions, and digital divides. Policy analysis examines frameworks such as the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) guidelines, balancing innovation with consumer protection in central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) like the Digital Euro and e-CNY. Business perspectives highlight competitive edges in supply chain optimization and tokenized economies, with practical recommendations for risk mitigation. Key applications explored include dynamic contract optimization using machine learning, AI oracles for trustless data integration, and AI-driven DAOs for governance. Institutional and retail use cases demonstrate AI-audited compliance and robo-advisors for portfolios. Regulatory and ethical challenges, including the legal personhood of AI-augmented DAOs and issues of bias, transparency, and accountability, are critically assessed. Future directions envision convergences with the Internet of Things (IoT) and quantum computing, fostering self-sustaining ecosystems amid risks such as encryption vulnerabilities and opportunities for trillions in value creation. Aimed at business professionals, academics, and regulators, the chapter provides actionable insights to navigate and profit from this evolving landscape, emphasizing ethical and sustainable practices.

Semantic communication offers a method for task-oriented information delivery in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled space networks, but compact semantic representations remain vulnerable to fading, noise, and structured corruption during transmission. This work proposes Clean–Impaired Semantic Preservation for Robust Semantic Communications (CISP-SemCom), a link-level semantic communication framework that explicitly learns from the clean latent representation and its communication-impaired counterpart generated from the same source sample. In a shared projection space, class-aware Clean–Impaired Contrastive Alignment (CI-Con) preserves cross-sample discrimination while excluding same-class non-matched samples from the negative set, and Semantic Preservation (SP) directly promotes consistency within each matched clean–impaired pair. In a ten-seed controlled same-backbone evaluation on CIFAR-10 under Rician fading, CISP-SemCom increases the normalized area under the robustness curve (AURC) evaluated over the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (SNR-AURC) from 66.85 ± 2.36 to 72.48 ± 1.24, corresponding to a paired gain of 5.63 AURC points with a 95% confidence interval of [3.75, 7.51]. Mechanism diagnostics show that SP-only optimization admits projector collapse, and that class-agnostic contrastive learning introduces same-class false-negative pressure. A direct class-aware ablation further indicates that most of the measured task-robustness gain comes from class-aware CI-Con, while SP acts as an explicit matched-pair consistency regularizer. On EuroSAT RGB, SNR-AURC increases from 65.53 ± 1.80 to 75.35 ± 1.58, showing that the robustness improvement is also observed on a second dataset. Decoder-independent latent probes further show improved accessibility of task-relevant class information, while the measured batch-1 inference latency remains similar to Backbone. These results support clean–impaired semantic preservation as an effective strategy for robust task-oriented transmission under satellite-inspired link impairments.

Background: The “2 Sigma Problem”, where individualized tutoring outperforms conventional instruction by two standard deviations, remains a persistent challenge in large-enrollment pharmacy courses. Generative AI tutors, constrained to instructor-verified content, offer a scalable, equitable approximation of personalized support. Methods: Four course-specific AI tutors were deployed across first-year (P1; n = 108–119/cohort) and third-year (P3; n = 98–108/cohort) Doctor of Pharmacy cohorts (Fall 2024–Spring 2026) using ChatGPT-4o and PlayLab with retrieval-augmented generation. Effectiveness was evaluated through longitudinal grade analysis, American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy proficiency outcomes, satisfaction surveys, and anonymized interaction log analysis. Results: Engagement was heterogeneous across curricular formats: 15-week P1 courses supported sustained weekly usage for foundational concept reinforcement, whereas 4-week P3 modules exhibited lower, targeted utilization focused on rapid self-assessment. In P1 Biochemistry, tutor integration was associated with longitudinal cohort exam improvements. The overall targeted metabolism exam mean rose from 74.0% (Fall 2023, no AI) to 81.4% (Fall 2024, AI tutor) and 83.6% (Fall 2025, AI tutor), with active users (n = 16, 85%, Fall 2024) outperforming non-users (n = 16, 79.3%, Fall 2024) by 5.7 percentage points, and with higher mean scores observed across progressively higher usage tiers. AACP proficiency means increased from 77.9% to 82.1%, exceeding the 80% benchmark. In P1 Physiology and P3 modules, cohort performance remained consistently high (83.7–88.2%), maintaining AACP benchmark proficiency across all observation cycles. Student perceptions were positive regarding conceptual clarification and adaptive explanations. Conclusions: Curriculum-aligned AI tutors represent a viable strategy for approximating individualized instruction in pharmacy courses. Course-specific AI tutors demonstrate feasibility across PharmD curricula, functioning as continuous retrieval-practice tools in foundational sciences and as targeted self-assessment aids in accelerated modules. Educational benefits and adoption dynamics are moderated by curricular pace, subject complexity, and assessment structures, highlighting key considerations for broader health sciences implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models in materials science are predominantly trained on ideal bulk crystals, limiting their transferability to real-world applications where surfaces, interfaces, and defects dominate. We present Mat3ra-2D, an open-source framework for the rapid design of realistic two-dimensional materials and related structures, including slabs and heterogeneous interfaces, with support for disorder and defect-driven complexity. The approach combines: (1) well-defined standards for storing and exchanging materials data with a modular implementation of core concepts and (2) transformation workflows expressed as configuration-builder pipelines that preserve provenance and metadata. We implement typical structure generation tasks, such as constructing orientation-specific slabs or strain-matching interfaces, in reusable Jupyter notebooks that serve as both interactive documentation and templates for reproducible runs. To lower the barrier to adoption, we design the examples to run in any web browser and demonstrate how to incorporate these developments into a web application. Mat3ra-2D enables systematic creation, provenance tracking, inspection, and reuse of realistic 2D- and interface-aware structures, providing the structure-generation layer needed for future AI/ML dataset construction for training.

In the fall of 2023, the Journal of the Medical Library Association (JMLA) introduced its policy on generative artificial intelligence (AI) submissions, predicting that these tools would become embedded within the workflows of clinicians, educators, researchers, and students. Those predictions dramatically underestimated AI's impact. On the three-year anniversary of that editorial, we revisit the issue in light of AI's unprecedentedly rapid adoption across knowledge work. We examine the educational challenges AI poses, arguing that excessive cognitive offloading threatens the deep thinking on which learning depends. We then consider the challenges AI creates for researchers, from hallucinated citations to fabricated diseases. We suggest that health sciences librarians, who offer expertise in approaching information systems with discernment, are well suited to be leaders in this space. To help prospective JMLA authors weigh whether and when to use AI, we propose the Compliance, Verifiability, and Disclosure (CVD) Framework. Throughout, we reaffirm our conviction that education and research must remain human-centered endeavors.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) renewed debates about who—or what—can legitimately contribute to democratic processes. While both AI and deliberative mini-publics can supplement citizens’ efforts to form judgments about issues, little is known about how citizens evaluate policy advice from these sources. In an online survey experiment with U.S. adults (N = 502), participants read a mock news story reporting a policy recommendation, attributed either to an AI system or a deliberative citizens’ assembly. Opinion climate was orthogonally varied to assess contextual influences. Results were split: citizens’ assemblies were rated fairer and more satisfying, but AI was perceived to be more useful. Opinion climate cues had no moderating effects. Further analysis indicated that acceptance of AI versus citizens’ assembly recommendations depends on individual factors, such as prior attitudes toward the issue and trust in AI. Findings offer theoretical and practical implications for designing democratic decision support systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

Alpiniae oxyphyllae Fructus (Zingiberaceae; Alpinia oxyphylla Miq) (AOF) is a traditional Chinese medicinal and edible homologous material rich in bioactive metabolites, including flavonoids, terpenes, and sesquiterpenes. Its multiple metabolites and multi-target nature confer unique advantages for cognitive function and neuroprotection. However, recent advances in extraction techniques, the discovery of AOF effects, and novel ameliorative mechanisms against Alzheimer’s disease (AD) require an updated review. This review systematically expands on the botanical features, traditional dietary applications, and quality control of AOF raw materials, as well as its AD-ameliorating effect, in vivo absorption, toxicological safety, and extraction technology optimization strategies. Moreover, we explored the emerging mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of AOF and its bioactive metabolites in improving AD, including effects on glial cell function, the gut–brain axis, brain metal ions, and advanced glycation end products. This review comprehensively summarizes preclinical studies, clinical research, and commercially available products related to AOF and its metabolites. It also expounds upon the potential impetus that artificial intelligence could offer AOF research in the future. In summary, this review provides innovative technologies, in-depth mechanistic analyses, and novel research directions for exploring AOF extracts and their bioactive metabolites to offer strategic guidance for identifying new functional factors and drug candidates to combat AD.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: To achieve optimal shielding performance of an active magnetic field (AMF), its shielding concept should be understood not as a hardware component but as an adaptive operational system. On a mission where radiation can vary quickly, resources will always be limited. Decisions can be made either automatically or under astronaut supervision. The idea behind the development of the AMF shielding described in this chapter is that of a human-in-the-loop (HITL) system in which astronauts' situational awareness, supervision, feedback from sensors, and the actuation of the magnetic field are integrated into a single adaptive protection scheme [1]. The development of the current chapter relies heavily on previous research related to the basic physical principles behind AMFs, trade-offs between shielding effectiveness and shielding material properties, secondary radiation, spacecraft charging, electromagnetic compatibility, and general considerations regarding risks within a larger system-of-systems architecture. The focus moves away from the technical feasibility of a subsystem toward a mission-oriented analysis of the potential of AMFs as radiation shields, including questions related to how effectively they will allow for mission adaptation while being compatible with astronaut decision-making under various conditions [2]. Three major threads run through the current chapter. First, this chapter explores the human-centered control architecture of AMF-based shielding, which describes how astronauts, sensors, supervising systems, and shielding subsystems work in conjunction to protect astronauts from space radiation [3]. Second, it studies the accumulated shielding effect as determined by time. In particular, the importance of cumulative dose reduction is emphasized, since shielding in deep space implies protection over the entire mission period, not just the instantaneous effectiveness of the shielding field [4]. Finally, the chapter provides an analysis of the energy consumption trade-off for different shielding modes [5].

Higher-education institutions devote a substantial share of their staff time to answering queries whose answers are already set out in institutional regulations. This paper presents the design and evaluation of an academic chatbot based on retrieval-augmented generation that lets users query those documents in natural language and receive grounded answers in Spanish. The system combines a structure-aware ingestion pipeline, a hybrid retriever that fuses dense semantic search and lexical search through reciprocal rank fusion, and a locally hosted large language model. A distinguishing goal is data sovereignty: every component runs on institutional hardware, so no data is sent to external services. Quality is evaluated with the RAGAS framework over five regulatory documents: the corpus-wide set attains a global score of 0.90, with faithfulness of 0.97. The acceptance criterion is not met, however, under its conjunctive reading: answer relevancy stays below its threshold across all sets, and p95 latency reaches 6.47 seconds against a 5-second target. Quality further degrades on long, heavily cross-referenced regulations. A contrast questionnaire administered to nineteen users places the perception index at 3.64 out of 5 and exposes a relevant discrepancy: only 57.9% agree that the system does not produce fabricated information, against the faithfulness the automatic judge assigns it.

Rapid and effective response to highway accidents is critical for reducing response delays and improving situational awareness. In this study, we present an agentic multi-drone, end-to-end incident management framework, developed and validated in the Gazebo simulation environment, in which specialized planning, coordination, perception, scene-description, and dispatch agents communicate through ROS/MAVROS and MQTT interfaces. A simulated emergency call transcript is processed by a GPT-4o mini-based planning agent to extract incident coordinates and mission intent, which the coordination agent resolves into an optimal drone-to-incident allocation. Up to four autonomous drones, each managed via MAVROS and ArduPilot, navigate under GUIDED mode to their assigned sites, where a custom-trained YOLOv11n perception agent performs real-time accident and fire recognition on live aerial imagery. Detected events trigger a fine-tuned BLIP-2 description agent, which converts visual evidence into structured natural-language incident reports. When multiple reports correspond to the same incident, confidence-prioritized fusion selects the highest-confidence view as the primary description and supplements it with non-duplicated salient information from secondary views. A Piper TTS-based dispatch agent then converts these summaries into audio alerts and autonomously routes them to the nearest rescue center based on drone proximity. The description agent was fine-tuned on 1,783 image–caption pairs derived from the curated incident dataset, with reference captions generated using moondream2, holding its visual encoder and Q-Former frozen to preserve pre-trained feature representations, and evaluated on a held-out set of 254 samples using BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, METEOR, CIDEr, and SPICE. Results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed modular agentic architecture for autonomous multi-incident perception, reasoning, and coordinated drone-based emergency response in the evaluated four-drone, four-incident simulation configuration. The framework provides a basis for future validation in larger-scale and real-world emergency-response scenarios.

Liver fibrosis is a global health concern where early detection is crucial for timely intervention. Traditional Chinese Medicine tongue diagnosis offers a promising non-invasive assessment, but suffers from inter-observer variability and subjective interpretation. Current artificial intelligence approaches focus on binary classification without revealing tongue features influencing diagnosis, limiting clinical utility. To address these challenges, we propose two key artificial intelligence innovations: (1) Hierarchical Kolmogorov–Arnold Network-based Adaptive Multi-task Experts, a novel multi-task learning architecture with adaptive quota routing that dynamically determines expert allocation based on sample complexity, solving the negative transfer problem; (2) Dynamic Tongue Relationship Graph Convolutional Network, a graph neural network that transforms expert selection patterns into patient-specific relationship graphs, enabling personalized modeling of attribute interactions. These artificial intelligence contributions advance the state-of-the-art in multi-task learning and dynamic graph construction for heterogeneous data, representing our core contributions at the artificial intelligence algorithmic level. As the engineering application of these artificial intelligence innovations, we develop Tongue Network with Dynamic Graph Relationship Learning, a non-invasive and interpretable framework based on tongue images that identifies seven critical tongue attributes and models their interrelationships for liver fibrosis risk screening in Traditional Chinese Medicine-based hepatology practice. Our method achieves 0.751 accuracy and 0.767 area under the curve, with 0.07 and 0.08 improvements over state-of-the-art graph neural networks and multimodal approaches. The framework offers visualizable classifications and relationship structures, providing insights into tongue features and liver fibrosis risk assessment. Codes are available at https://github.com/MedAI-UAIX/TongueNet-DGRL .
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Abstract Manufacturing industry is being increasingly forced to go green without compromising on the efficiency and effectiveness of their operations. This paper discusses an artificial intelligence based approach for encouraging the adoption of green practices in the manufacturing industries. Green manufacturing is an essential way of attaining environmental sustainability. However, the adoption of green manufacturing is still a challenge owing to the problem of reconciling the economic objectives with the environmental requirements. The integration of machine learning and green manufacturing results into a decision support system. The AI model designed utilizes predictive analytics, neural networks, and optimization algorithms for the identification of green manufacturing opportunities and for the formulation of strategies for their implementation. The data used comes from 85 manufacturing plants of the automotive, electronics, and textile industries, which proves the effectiveness of the model. The results show that AI-assisted green manufacturing reaches up to 27% less energy use, 22% material waste reduction, and 25% lower carbon footprint so far comparing with the traditional methods. The model is going to be a source of support and practical advice for the manufacturers, who are willing to be environmentally responsible and perform operatively, thus, the research will add to and share the existing academic knowledge of sustainable manufacturing along with the industrial part of the practice.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In high-tech research and development (R&D) contexts, where artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tools and digital collaboration platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent, the learning and integration pathways of newly hired R&D employees are undergoing structural changes. Mentorship has emerged as a key mechanism supporting organizational socialization and innovation. This study examines the role of mentorship as a core mechanism in integrating internal digital platforms and cross-departmental resources to construct a systematic organizational socialization support network. Adopting a qualitative, cross-sectional single-case study strategy, this study collected data through semi-structured interviews and internal archival documents and analyzed the data using directed content analysis. This study finds that G Automobile Group embeds mentorship into its “180-Day Transformation Program,” thereby forming a closed-loop development system through growth planning, dynamic feedback, and regular reviews. By combining contextualized on-the-job mentoring with resource-based self-directed learning, mentorship facilitates the transformation of tacit knowledge into job competence. A hierarchical mentoring system, knowledge accumulation through digital platforms, and cross-departmental resource integration further enhance the effectiveness of newcomer socialization. The study also finds that mentors serve dual roles as supporters and evaluators. Transparent standards and clear communication processes are required to reduce the risk of negative mentoring experiences. The novelty of this study lies in conceptualizing mentorship not merely as a dyadic support relationship but as a digitally embedded organizational socialization support system that integrates formal mentoring, informal resource flows, AI-enabled tools, and cross-departmental collaboration.

Routine forest-road maintenance is essential for road safety, accessibility, and serviceability, yet current inspections remain labor-intensive. Existing visual methods usually quantify pavement distresses independently, which may introduce area-estimation errors and affect condition assessment when multiple distresses spatially overlap. To address this engineering challenge, this study proposes an engineering artificial intelligence framework integrating Transformer-based semantic segmentation and diffusion-based data augmentation for unmanned aerial vehicle-assisted multi-distress measurement, overlapping-distress quantification, and forest-road condition assessment. This framework incorporates a segmentation model that converts aerial images into pixel-level distress masks for area measurement. The segmentation model employs a dynamic-gated convolutional backbone to integrate local textures with global context and a frequency-modulated spatial attention decoder to enhance small-scale and weakly visible distresses. A two-stage overlapping-distress identification strategy is developed to localize overlapping regions, identify their constituent distress categories, and support overlap-aware area quantification and condition assessment. A multi-condition guided diffusion model is further introduced to enrich inspection-image diversity, and a Forest Road Daily Inspection dataset is constructed for model training and evaluation. For engineering assessment, a Forest Pavement Condition Index is developed by incorporating measured areas of multiple distress types and overlapping regions, enabling section-level condition evaluation and maintenance prioritization. Experiments on the constructed forest-road inspection dataset and a public benchmark demonstrate that the proposed segmentation model improves multi-distress segmentation, overlapping-region identification, and measurement-oriented condition assessment, supporting its potential for forest-road condition measurement and maintenance-oriented assessment under the tested conditions.

Many resource-constrained edge devices require artificial intelligence (AI) services but are not powerful enough to store or execute neural networks (NNs). Analog radio frequency (RF) computing addresses this limitation by letting a base station (BS) multicast a waveform encoding NN weights to different clients. Each client then multiplies the received weight-encoded waveform with its locally generated input-encoded waveform through a passive mixer in its RF frontend, thereby realizing the matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) needed for AI inference with an extremely low power and memory requirement. This can enable telecom operators to provide AI inference services to the edge devices connected to their networks. In practice, however, this multicast AI flow must share the spectrum, power, and spatial resources with other data flows. This paper considers a multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) downlink scenario and studies the resulting relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating the multicast AI flow with the unicast data flows. We formulate a joint beamforming problem for the data and AI flows to maximize the aggregate data rate subject to computing accuracy, client energy, total power, and hardware-related constraints. We develop a weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE)-based algorithm to solve the problem. Numerical results based on 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) channels show that the relative aggregate data rate reduction from integrating an AI flow with data flows is below 5% in representative settings. This indicates that telecom operators can use analog RF computing to provide edge AI services while providing data communication services simultaneously.

This study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) use affects students' critical thinking skills in learning. The study uses a quantitative, explanatory research design. The study population consisted of students in the Economics Education Study Program who used AI-based applications for learning. The study collected data through a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire from 64 respondents who met the research criteria. The researchers analyzed the data using validity and reliability tests, assumption tests, and simple linear regression in SPSS. The results show that using AI has a positive and significant effect on students' critical thinking skills. The t-test yielded t = 4.670 (p = 0.000), and the regression coefficient was 0.431. The R-square value of 0.260 indicates that AI use explains 26% of the variation in students' critical thinking skills, while other factors account for the remaining 74%. These findings suggest that appropriate AI use can support students' ability to analyze, evaluate, and solve problems.

Background Rupture of unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIA) is the third leading cause of morbidity and mortality from cerebrovascular disease, with a disability rate as high as 36–58%; health behaviors are crucial for reducing the risk of rupture. Protection Motivation Theory serves as an effective framework for explaining the formation of health behaviors; however, there is currently a lack of analyses on the latent categories of protection motivation for health behaviors among UIA patients both domestically and internationally, and in-depth exploration of population heterogeneity and intrinsic motivation has been neglected. Based on Protection Motivation Theory, this study explores the overall level and dimensional characteristics of protection motivation for health behaviors among UIA patients, analyzes its latent profiles and influencing factors, and provides a reference for clinical stratified management and personalized interventions. Methods From July to December 2025, a convenience sample of 300 UIA patients meeting the inclusion criteria was recruited from a Grade A tertiary hospital in Jiangxi Province for a clinical survey. A self-designed general demographic questionnaire, the UIA Patient Health Behavior Protective Motivation Scale, and the Health Promotion Lifestyle Scale II (HPLP-II) were used to assess the current status of health behavior protective motivation, health-promoting lifestyles, and their relationship among UIA patients. This study employed latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify latent profiles among UIA patients. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare differences in general demographic data and disease-related scores across latent profiles. Chi-square tests and Fisher’s exact test were used for categorical variables. Pearson correlation analysis was used to examine the relationship between protection motivation and health-promoting behaviors. Multinomial logistic regression was used to investigate the factors influencing these latent profiles. Results The results of this study showed that the total score for health behavior protection motivation among UIA patients was (81.96 ± 15.41) points, and the total score for health behavior promotion was (126.83 ± 30.78) points. The total score for health behavior protection motivation was positively correlated with the total scores of the HPLP-II and the HPLP-II ( r = 0.73, p < 0.001),and the total scores of each dimension were positively correlated with the total score for health behavior promotion ( p < 0.001). One-way ANOVA revealed significant differences in HPLP-II total scores across the three latent profiles ( F (2, 297) = 136.459, p < 0.001). Chi-square tests showed significant differences in educational level, sleep quality, smoking, alcohol consumption, and comorbid chronic diseases across the three groups ( χ 2 = 7.693–60.171, df = 2–4, all p < 0.05). This study identified three latent profiles of protective motivation: the low protective motivation group (21.0%), the moderate protective motivation group (53.0%), and the high protective motivation group (26.0%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis showed that educational level (OR = 6.997, 95% CI: 2.053–23.850), sleep quality (OR = 5.069, 95% CI: 1.644–15.626), and HPLP-II total score (OR = 1.078, 95% CI: 1.051–1.105) were facilitators for the moderate group, while smoking (OR = 0.357, 95% CI: 0.138–0.928) and alcohol consumption (OR = 0.103, 95% CI: 0.053–0.201) were barriers. For the high group, educational level (OR = 8.010, 95% CI: 1.855–34.597) and HPLP-II total score (OR = 1.147, 95% CI: 1.113–1.183) were facilitators, while alcohol consumption (OR = 0.101, 95% CI: 0.047–0.218) was a barrier. Conclusion The total scores for health behavior protection and motivation, and the total HPLP-II scores, among UIA patients were generally moderate. Furthermore, health behavior protection motivation exhibited heterogeneity and could be classified into three distinct latent profiles. Clinically, personalized intervention plans can be developed based on the characteristics and latent profiles of patients, with the aim of enhancing patients’ levels of health behavior protection motivation, improving health-promoting behaviors, reducing the risk of aneurysm rupture, and improving long-term disease prognosis.

Proactive AI can make domestic products more responsive while raising concerns about unwanted intervention, control, and privacy. This study examines anticipated acceptance of AI-proactive smart sofas through a value–reactance framework. A theory-guided exploratory sequential mixed-methods design combinedinterviews with 10 prospective users and a scenario-based survey of 401 valid cases. PLS-SEM showed that perceived AI proactivity was positively associated with perceived usefulness and perceived intrusiveness, although the usefulness-related coefficient was substantially larger. Perceived usefulness was positively associated with AI trust and behavioral intention, whereas perceived intrusiveness was positively associated with psychological reactance, which was negatively associated with AI trust and behavioral intention. Privacy sensitivity positively moderated the intrusiveness–reactance association, although the interaction was small. Because participants evaluated a hypothetical product rather than interacting with an actual sofa, behavioral intention is interpreted as anticipated acceptance rather than observed adoption. The findings highlight user control, transparency, and privacy as design considerations.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

Abstract STUDY QUESTION How many mature oocytes are biologically required to achieve at least three euploid blastocysts, by maternal age and AI-derived oocyte quality, and how does this estimate compare with real-world oocyte yields in elective fertility preservation? SUMMARY ANSWER Required oocyte numbers rise steeply with advancing maternal age and decreasing AI-derived oocyte quality, and the median number cryopreserved per fertility preservation cycle falls progressively below estimated requirements, by 12- to 30-fold in women older than 40 years. WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY Elective oocyte cryopreservation is increasingly used to preserve future reproductive potential, but counselling typically relies on uniform age-based oocyte targets that do not account for inter-individual variability in oocyte biological competence. Although AI-based oocyte assessment has shown promise as an objective adjunct to morphological evaluation, no biologically integrated framework has been used to translate AI-derived oocyte quality into a quantitative requirement-versus-yield comparison in fertility preservation. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION Retrospective cohort study with probabilistic modelling of blastulation and euploidy, using three datasets from a single private university-affiliated IVF centre. Model development used 13,782 mature oocytes from 1,625 autologous ICSI cycles (1,020 patients, 2021–2024) and 3,325 biopsied embryos with conclusive PGT-A results (857 patients). External validation was performed in 1,948 oocytes from 333 ovum donation cycles in 271 donors (2020–2024). Real-world application used 1,647 elective fertility preservation cycles in 1,100 patients between 2012 and 2024. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS Each oocyte was scored using a commercially available artificial-intelligence image-analysis system that assigns a 0–10 oocyte quality score. Blastulation and euploidy were modelled by logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors. The integrated probabilistic framework computed the minimum number of mature oocytes required to obtain at least three euploid blastocysts at a probability of 90% or greater, by maternal age category and tertile of AI-derived oocyte quality score. Model-derived requirements were compared with the median number of oocytes actually cryopreserved per fertility preservation cycle. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE Blastulation increased with higher AI-derived oocyte quality score (OR 1.19 per point, 95% CI 1.18–1.21; P < 0.001) and decreased with maternal age (OR 0.94 per year, 95% CI 0.93–0.96; P < 0.001); the oocyte quality effect was externally validated in donors (OR 1.11 per point, 95% CI 1.08–1.14). Euploidy declined non-linearly with age, from 68.6% (<30 years) to 19.3% (>40 years). Estimated mature-oocyte requirements ranged from 9 (95% CI 8–11) at < 30 years with high AI-derived oocyte quality to 121 (104–146) at > 40 years with low AI-derived oocyte quality. The median number cryopreserved per cycle decreased from 8.3 at < 30 to 4.0 at > 40 years and fell progressively below estimated requirements; in women older than 40 years the observed yield was 12- to 30-fold below the estimated requirement. LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION Blastulation and euploidy probabilities were derived from autologous ICSI cycles in patients with infertility-related indications; extrapolation to elective fertility preservation candidates assumes that per-oocyte biological competence, conditional on age and AI-derived quality, is transportable across populations. The probabilistic framework assumes conditional independence between blastulation and euploidy. The model estimates oocyte requirements for euploid blastocyst formation but does not directly model implantation, clinical pregnancy, or live birth. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS The divergence between observed yields and model-derived requirements is best interpreted not as a deficiency in retrieval practice but as an individualised benchmark. Integrating AI-based oocyte assessment with age-specific euploidy probabilities may support more personalised, biologically informed counselling, expectation-setting, and care planning, particularly for women considering oocyte cryopreservation after the mid-thirties. FUNDING This research did not receive any specific grant from public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agencies. DISCLOSURES J.F. and P.M. are employees of Future Fertility, the developer of the artificial-intelligence oocyte-scoring system used in this study. The remaining authors declare no competing interests. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER N/A
